summary: California City is technically the third-largest city in California — by land area. At nearly 204 square miles, it sprawls larger than San Jose, yet holds barely 13,000 residents, yielding a strikingly sparse 65 people per square mile across a vast grid of empty, unpaved streets originally platted in the 1950s as a speculative desert metropolis that never materialized. Sitting on the western edge of the Mojave Desert northeast of Edwards Air Force Base — a major local employer alongside correctional facilities — the landscape is flat, wind-scoured, and wide open, with unobstructed views of the Tehachapi Mountains to the north and endless high-desert sky delivering roughly 10.7 hours of daily sunshine and summer highs that routinely push well past the 77°F annual average. Housing costs reflect the isolation: a median home value around $239,600 against a median household income of $55,271 produces a price-to-income ratio under 4.4, genuinely affordable by California standards, though a 24.3% poverty rate signals the local economy offers limited upward mobility. Retail and dining options are minimal, grocery runs can require real distance, and the nearest significant urban center is Lancaster, about 25 miles south. California City is less a functioning town than a monument to mid-century ambition still waiting for its population to arrive.
